newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia property clampdown seen to avoid bubble.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia property clampdown seen to avoid bubble.

text.p: Worries over a potential property glut in Malaysia and the painful lesson experienced by neighbouring Thailand were behind the central bank's moves to curb speculative loans, analysts said on Monday.
Bank Negara's clampdown on loans for buying property battered property and banking stocks on Monday but the analysts saw a silver lining in the long-term.

"It looks like Bank Negara is trying to take action before (what happened in Thailand) actually happens here. The trend of overheating is not completely squeezed out of the economy," said Kevin Chew, economist at Caspian Research.
Thailand has been battling a financial crisis for weeks caused by oversupply in the property sector, high interest rates and the slowest economic growth in a decade.
Memories still linger about Malaysia's own property bubble in the mid-1980s, which helped trigger a recession and saw the central bank bailing out some commercial banks.

In releasing its 1996 annual report on Friday, the central bank announced it will limit to 20 percent a bank's outstanding loans to the property sector from April 1. Loans for properties valued 150,000 ringgit ($60,483) and below are exempted.
Bank Negara also further restricted credit for buying stocks.
The annual report said loans to the property sector had now reached 30 percent of all commercial loans.
Analysts said nine years of more than eight percent annual economic growth had raised expectations in the property market that the good times would just keep on rolling.
But they warned that a property glut was looming in and around capital Kuala Lumpur, especially in the office sector.
"There's oversupply in shopping malls and offices. Hotels are also oversupplied," said Phuah Lee Kerk, head of research at Jupiter Securities.

In a recent report, the government's Valuation and Property Services Department said property transactions grew by 23 percent last year, slower than 1995's 34 percent growth. It also warned of a "slight glut" in office properties.

The government estimated that Kuala Lumpur will have 2.03 million square metres of new office space by 1999, bringing the total to about 5.6 million square metres. Analysts say annual take-up demand is around 278,000 square metres.

"You can roughly see that there will be oversupply. Occupancy will drop to 60-65 percent. At that point some people will go under," said Edward Ong, property analyst at Schroder Research. He said office building owners need at least 65 percent occupancy to break even. Current office space occupancy is about 95 percent.
Retail space is already oversupplied at 400,000 square metres but another 1.8 million square feet is planned over the next four years, according to official statistics.
Stocks of property developers and banks skidded on the central bank news as investors anticipate that property prices will consolidate after the clampdown.

"I think the stockmarket is ready to move up again after this week when foreign investors see that Malaysia is aware of a problem and are taking measures, and it is not like Thailand," said Phuah at Jupiter Securities.

At 0350 GMT on Monday, the Kuala Lumpur Stock Exchange (KLSE) Property Index plunged 85.85 points or 3.12 percent to 2,667.09. The Financial Index dropped 339.20 points or 3.12 percent also to 10,534.30.
-- Kuala Lumpur newsroom (603-201 4813)
($1 = 24.8 ringgit)
